claims: An English-held fortified town with surrounding march was governed and supplied by the English Crown until its recapture by France in 1558.
The Calais Pale was a small frontier district; not all the areas shown on broader 1558 maps of Calais and Boulogne were English-controlled in 1500.

claims: Grummitt scholarly monograph describes distinct regular garrisons at Calais town and castle, Guînes, Hammes and Rysbank.

These named places are strongly supported station candidates, but a list of fortresses is not a connected territorial polygon and modern point coordinates would require separate historic site location checking.

claims: Secondary scholarly account citing the Calendar of Close Rolls Henry VII 1500–1509 p.99 reports Henry VII ordered Guînes peacetime garrison limited to 60 men instead of 100.
The same account reports expected reduction in wage bill of 500 marks annually earmarked for repairs of the castle.
An authorized budget reduction is not evidence that those savings became cash remitted to England, nor evidence that the projected sum accrued for the decade.
remaining: Read actual Calendar of Close Rolls 1500–1509 p99 and archival roll
Distinguish marks of money (not £ sterling) and annual wage budget order from realized annual cash

claims: English staple merchants and Crown paid for the garrison and defense using revenues generated from English wool exports through Calais.
Early 16th century export contraction increased the difficulty of meeting defense costs.
This mechanism does not give a trustworthy number for Calais fiscal net benefit to the Crown; wool shipment gross value, staple charges, and garrison outlays must be reconciled separately.
remaining: Extract DL28 and E36 for matching regnal years
Find customs E122 and staple E364 and repeatable nominal accounting categories
Never treat military fiscal savings as export income

claims: Several surviving official catalogued maps have secure later dates, e.g. 1545 Thomas Pettyt outskirts and Nicolay 1558 map.

Published 1558 map, reprinted 1592, would be anachronistic if directly used as 1500 English Pale polygon.
